claims.claim: Daoism (also spelled Taoism) is a family of Chinese traditions — philosophical, religious, and cultural — centered on the Dao, usually translated 'the Way'; the Dao is described as the ultimate creative principle of the universe in which all things are unified and connected.
The Dao is not a personal god in the manner of the Abrahamic religions; Daoism includes many deities that are worshipped in temples and are understood as part of the universe, dependent on the Dao.

The distinction between philosophical Daoism (centered on the Daodejing and Zhuangzi) and religious Daoism (deities, ritual, longevity practices) is a scholarly convention that is contested: Britannica calls the split a descriptive convenience, BBC calls the textbook distinction artificial, and the SEP quotes sinologist Kristofer Schipper calling it a 'sinological dogma'; premodern Chinese had no words corresponding to 'philosophy' and 'religion'.

The Daodejing ('Classic of the Way and Its Power', also known as the Tao Te Ching or Laozi) is a short text of about 5,000 Chinese characters in 81 brief chapters of dense aphoristic passages; it is traditionally attributed to Laozi but was probably compiled from the sayings of many people over time, reaching its familiar form around the 3rd century BCE.

The Zhuangzi, attributed to Zhuang Zhou (Zhuangzi, 'Master Zhuang', c. 369-286 BCE) and partly composed by his disciples, is a longer and more literary work of stories, dialogues, and paradoxes, described by Britannica as more comprehensive than the Daodejing.

Wu wei is 'uncontrived action' or 'natural non-intervention' — acting in accord with the natural course of things rather than forcing outcomes; the translation 'non-action' wrongly implies that nothing gets done.
Ziran ('naturalness' or 'spontaneity') names the condition of being naturally so — the state something reaches when permitted to exist and develop naturally without interference.

Yin and yang describe the world as filled with complementary polar forces — action and non-action, light and dark, hot and cold — whose balance sustains harmony; the yin-yang symbol and the concept of polar forces are central Daoist ideas.

Daoist practice includes meditation for mental stillness and mindfulness, qigong breathing and movement exercises that cultivate qi (the vital energy understood to flow through the body), and temple ritual with purification, offerings to deities, chanting, and the jiao, a rite of cosmic renewal.

Historically, Daoists practiced alchemy: external alchemy (waidan) sought elixirs from minerals and herbs to promote long life, and internal alchemy (neidan) sought to transform the practitioner through meditation and inner cultivation; terms meaning 'long life' and 'immortality' are among the most recurrent in Daoist literature.

In Chinese religious life, Daoism has long coexisted and blended with Confucianism and Buddhism: since Song times (960-1279) Daoist and Buddhist elements have coexisted in folk religion without clear distinctions in the minds of worshippers, and the Daoist tradition has often served as a link between the Confucian tradition and folk tradition.

Daoism today: Daoist temples, monasteries, and priests remain active in China and Taiwan, where Daoism functions like a conventional religion, while Daoist-derived practices such as taiji and qigong have spread worldwide, often as secular health and exercise routines.

positions: Britannica: since Han times scholars distinguished daojia (a Daoist philosophy of the great mystics) from daojiao (a later Daoist religion), but this theory is 'no longer considered valid'; the article makes the split 'simply for the sake of descriptive convenience'
BBC Religions: the textbook distinction between 'religious' and 'philosophical' Taoism is 'an artificial distinction', no more than the gap between any religion's practices and its ideas

SEP Religious Daoism (quoting Kristofer Schipper): distinguishing the 'Taoist school' from the 'Taoist religion' has become a 'sinological dogma'; the Daoist canons never made it, and the terms are practically synonymous and interchangeable
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both strands as scholarly categories, explicitly names the distinction as scholarly and contested, and teaches the contested status itself as part of the content.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Authorship and dating of the Daodejing
positions: BBC Religions: the Tao Te Ching was compiled around the 3rd century BCE; no one person wrote it
Britannica: the earliest work of Daoist philosophy, traditionally attributed to Laozi but probably composed after his death by many authors
SEP Religious Daoism: compiled in a form close to the received text probably in the late 3rd century BCE
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says the text is traditionally attributed to Laozi but was probably compiled from the sayings of many people over time, reaching its familiar form around the third century BCE, and never assigns single authorship.

positions: BBC Religions: the Tao itself is not God, nor a god, nor is it worshipped by Taoists; Taoists venerate many deities
Britannica: the Daoist religion is 'concerned with the ritual worship of the Dao'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson avoids adjudicating the phrase 'worship of the Dao': it states that the Dao is not a personal god, describes the many deities worshipped in temples, and describes religious Daoism's ritual life without asserting that the Dao itself is an object of worship.

positions: Britannica: Daoism and Confucianism present contrasting, though not incompatible, understandings of human flourishing; the traditions share many ideas about man, society, and the ruler
OpenStax: 'whereas Confucianism is concerned with day-to-day rules of conduct, Taoism is concerned with a more spiritual level of being'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes the relationship as contrast without simple opposition, noting both the differing emphases and the centuries of coexistence and blending.

sourceRecords.provider: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Michel Strickmann and Roger T. Ames)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read via an Internet Archive capture of 2024-09-21 (web.archive.org/web/20240921011814/https://www.britannica.com/topic/Daoism) because britannica.com blocks automated fetch. Supports: Daoism as comprising the ideas of the Daodejing, Zhuangzi, and related writings, the Daoist religion concerned with ritual worship of the Dao, and those who identify as Daoists; the daojia/daojiao distinction since Han times with the older theory 'no longer considered valid' and the philosophical/religious split made 'simply for the sake of descriptive convenience'; Laozi as founding figure flourishing in the 6th century BCE about whom little else is known; the Daodejing as the earliest work of Daoist philosophy, traditionally attributed to Laozi but probably composed after his death by many authors; Zhuangzi (369-286 BCE) and his work, partly composed by his disciples, as more comprehensive than the Daodejing; the Daoism/Confucianism contrast (harmony between the human way and the natural order vs moral excellence within social institutions); the Daoist tradition as often serving as a link between the Confucian tradition and folk tradition; coexistence of Daoist and Buddhist elements in folk religion since Song times without clear distinctions; Chan (Zen) as an essentially Chinese development inside Buddhism; influence on Vietnam, Japan, and Korea. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.provider: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live from plato.stanford.edu on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Entry first published 2025. Supports: dao (path, way) as the central Daoist concept; Laozi and Zhuangzi as founding personages who did not coin the '-ism', with the two classical texts emerging in the Classical period (5th-3rd century BCE); the terms for the Daoist school (daojia) and its teachings (daojiao) both coined during the Han dynasty; ziran (self-so, natural, spontaneous) as the way the Dao comes to have its structure of itself; qi as material energy, breath; the classical Yin-Yang school; Daoism's skeptical engagement with the Confucian-Mohist debate; Buddhism's introduction to China with Laozi worship adopting institutional structures from Buddhism and the convergence into Chan (Zen) Buddhism; Wang Bi curating the received Laozi (Daode Jing) and Guo Xiang the Zhuangzi. Facts synthesized in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: Religious Daoism
sourceRecords.provider: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live from plato.stanford.edu on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Entry by Fabrizio Pregadio (first published 2016, substantive revision 2020). Supports: Kristofer Schipper's statement that distinguishing the 'Taoist school' (Daojia) from the 'Taoist religion' (Daojiao) has become a 'sinological dogma' never made by the Daoist canons (Daozang), where the terms are practically synonymous and interchangeable; premodern Chinese having no words for 'philosophy' or 'religion', with Daoists speaking instead of the 'lineage of the Dao' (daojia) and the 'teachings of the Dao' (daojiao); Daoism as a tradition as complex and heterogeneous as Buddhism, Islam, Judaism, or Christianity; the Way of the Celestial Masters (Tianshi dao), founded per tradition in 142 CE when Lord Lao appeared to Zhang Daoling, today one of the two main branches of Daoism under the name Way of the Correct Unity (Zhengyi dao); the Daode jing as the source of the Daoist tradition; fangshi ('masters of the methods') from the 4th century BCE practicing cosmological arts, medicine, alchemy, and longevity practices; 'nourishing life' (yangsheng) including daoyin, breathing, and sexual practices, with present-day practices often defined as Daoist such as Qigong and Taiji quan belonging to this category; terms meaning 'long life' and 'immortality' among the most recurrent in Daoist literature; external alchemy (waidan) and internal alchemy (neidan), with herbal medicines granting long life and elixirs granting immortality in classical framings. Facts synthesized in original wording.
